utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. It seems to me that you are new. Would you introduce yourself for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My name is Milbert Shin and I will be appearing for the Prosecution today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Shin, you may begin your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, could you please tell the Trial Chamber your full name?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's Kathryn Jean Barr.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I'm a forensic document examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And where are you based.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: In Birmingham in the U.K.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I will be speaking a little bit more slowly, not to tax the interpreters too much at the beginning of the day. Where are you employed currently?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I'm employed at a company called Document Evidence Limited which is based in Birmingham.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What position do you hold there?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I'm a director of the company and a forensic document examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, has the Prosecution requested you to conduct two handwriting comparisons?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It has, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please make a pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Shin. Since you and the witness are speaking the same language, I would like to ask you to slow a down a little bit, because we missed something in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. I will maybe back up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And begin very slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I am of course open to cautions of speeding up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I'm a forensic document examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And where are you based?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I'm based at a company called Document Evidence Limited, which is in Birmingham in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what position do you hold at document evidence limited?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I'm a director of the company and I'm a forensic document examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, did the Prosecution request you to conduct two handwriting comparisons?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you provided documents for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher. This is a document which has previously been entered into evidence in this case. Exhibit P133.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you could turn to the first red tab there. Could you please take a look at that page and the pages up to the second red tab. Do you recognise those pages?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And are those the pages that you were provided for the purposes of your document examination?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record that is ERN pages 02935743 through 02935753. These are pages from the duty officer's unofficial workbook, which, as I noted earlier, has the Exhibit Number P133.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, before we get to your analysis and any conclusions or findings you may have made as a result of that analysis, I'd like to ask you first about your training and experience; and secondly, I'd like to ask you if you could explain to us the field of handwriting comparison and the methodology involved. If we could begin with your training and experience. What is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I've got a bachelor of arts degree and also a Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What year did you receive your Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what did you do immediately after your -- receiving your Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: As soon as I finished by Ph.D., I started work as a forensic document examiner at the Metropolitan Police Forensics Science Laboratory in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How many years did you work there?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I worked there until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I transferred to the forensic science service laboratory in Wetherby until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And were you still a forensic document examiner at that point?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And how long were you at that institute?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I moved on from there in November 1999 to join my present company, Document Evidence Limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Where -- as you have already explained to us you are a forensic document examiner?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, what does a forensic document examiner do? What sorts of tasks does a forensic document examiner do, for example?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: We do many -- basically, any examinations involved with documents that have been involved in -- that are in dispute, so that includes handwriting and signature comparisons, looking for alterations and obliterations, indent impressions, looking for type writing, printing methods, counterfeiting of documents, generally a whole gamut of examinations that could involve -- in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Would a forensic document examiner have a specialisation among those tasks that you've just listed for us?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No. Within the United Kingdom a forensic document examiner is involved in the totality of those examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you yourself have undertaken all of those tasks?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, how does one become a forensic document examiner? Is this something that you can study at university to become?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: There are now forensic examination courses. There wasn't when I was at university. Generally the only way to become a forensic document examiner is to undertake a period of training within a forensic document establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And how long would that period of training typically be?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Typically it would be two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you yourself undertake such a training period?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And where did you undertake your training?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: At the Metropolitan Police Forensics Science Laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you explained earlier is that in London. Can you -- could you please just explain to us just briefly what you do as an apprentice -- someone who's in training, let's say?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Generally you start off with an initial period whereby you are taught the basic principles of document examination, so that you know what sort of examinations are undertaken. But then, most -- you then move on to shadowing other experienced document examiners, undertaking small parts of cases for them, all within the supervision. And then gradually over the period of the years you do more and more of your own work under less and less supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: During your period of training, did you undertake handwriting comparisons?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you have been a forensic document examiner now for 12 years, is that correct, from 1993, I believe you said --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. During those 12 years how many handwriting comparisons have you done?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I've done over a thousand cases. Within those cases, there could be many different handwriting comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And could you please describe just briefly what sorts of documents were involved in those comparisons.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Literally any type of document at all: Cheques, forms, letters. Any type of handwriting on any type of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And these handwriting comparisons, who have you done them for?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: We work for police forces, but also for banks, building societies, insurance companies, government agencies such as customs and excise, inland revenue, human resources, departments of companies, and for members of the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, have you previously given evidence in court on the basis of your document examination work?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Approximately how many times would you say you've done that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: For handwriting comparisons, probably 20, 25 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the course of your career as a document -- forensic document examiner, are there other professional activities that you undertake in addition to your work?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I'm also involved with going to conferences, writing articles, and also looking at research collaboration with university departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you have any accreditations as a document forensic -- forensic document examiner?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: There are very few accreditations available for a forensic document examiner. A new body that's been set up within the United Kingdom is the council for the registration of forensic practitioners. And I am accredited by that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Barr, I'm now going to ask you to explain the field about handwriting analysis and comparison and also to give us some explanation of the methodology involved in that. But I'd like to begin by asking you first to give us a brief definition of handwriting. What is handwriting?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Handwriting is a human skill, whereby character shapes are generated by use of a writing implement as a visual representation of language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the -- I'll just pause for a minute to make sure the translation is there. In the field of handwriting comparison or handwriting analysis, are there -- what are the principles -- what are the fundamental concepts of that field?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: The basic principle on which it is based is that given sufficient writings, no two people will write in exactly the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And are there other principles or underlying tenets that would guide your analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: The main principle is that handwriting comparison can only be undertaken with a like-for-like comparison. By that, I mean that it involves individual comparisons of characters, but a block -- an upper case A can only be compared with other upper case As, not with lower case examples of that letter, and obviously not with other letters. There are other features involved, and that's -- in any handwriting comparison, even between two different people, there will be some similarities, because character shapes can't -- have to conform to recognised designs for writing to be readable. And so simply by chance, some features will always be similar. And similarly, even within the writings of one person, things will be different because human beings aren't machines and don't reproduce things exactly. So there will be a range of variation between writings done on different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Broadly speaking, what is handwriting comparison? What is it that you do when you're comparing handwritings?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It involves a systematic step-by-step approach going through the writings that you've been asked to compare to look at each character in turn to determine how that character has been constructed, and by that I mean how the pen has moved across the paper to construct it, and then to look at other features, for example, fluency, slope, proportion, connectiveness, all the other features associated with those characters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I ask you to explain further. Is there a particular order in which you go about this? Would you look at both sets of documents that you're trying to compare?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Generally you would choose either the writing that you've been provided that's questioned or the writing that you've been provided with a specimen. You take one of those two types of writing and go through that in turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You were explaining to us about this step-by-step approach and looking at the way each character is constructed. You used some terms and I would like you to please explain what some of those terms mean to us. First you used the term "fluency." What is that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Fluency is the speed with which the handwriting has been written. Most practiced writers write fluently at some speed. This can be determined by looking for things such as variation in pen pressure and tapered ends to strokes. By that I mean that when you're coming to the end of a stroke, you know that you're coming to the end of that stroke, and so you will start lifting the pen from the paper before the stroke is finished. And this leads to a tapered end to it. By contrast, if you ended the stroke and then abruptly lifted the pen from the paper, the end of that stroke would be very blunt, and therefore, you can tell the difference between writing that's been written at speed and stuff that's been written more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also used the word "slope," and what is that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's an indication of whether the writing is upright or leans forwards or backwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you mentioned a couple other features that you look at. And what are those?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Proportions, which would be the variation of the size of characters, both within the proportions of the character itself and also within a word. And also connectiveness, which is how one character is connected on to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you say that you do this by going through the character -- individual characters?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, in a step-by-step approach, working through the alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Does that mean you do it letter by letter then?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is there some way that you document or maintain records of your analysis as you proceed through this?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Generally we make notes of actually drawing out the characters when we determine their construction on a piece of paper that we call a tick sheet, which is basically a piece of paper with the alphabet written out on it so that it ensures that you go through in a systematic and methodical approach, documenting all the features that you find.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And this document that you call a tick sheet, if one were to look at that, would that capture the totality of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No. Obviously it can only be an aide-memoire because what you are trying to do an assess the range of variation of each character in the writing. Obviously it's not possible or reasonable to have to draw every single character, when many will only vary by a small amount. So you use it as an aide-memoire, so that, for example, when you have to come to court you can remember what are the salient features that you thought were important in a particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And this process of examining each set of writings and producing this tick sheet as part of your analysis, I gather this is something you do for both sets of documents?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: After you've gone through this stage of examining both sets of documents, what's the next thing that you do as a forensic document examiner?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: At this point you will have -- for each set of writing you will have a range of variation for each character. It's then important to look at those two ranges of variation and assess how similar or how different they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you just explain that a little further. When you say "range of variation," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: What I mean is that, as I've said before, when -- because people vary when they write, each character they produce isn't exactly the same as the other one but -- as one they produced before, but they will only vary within a defined range. The idea of looking through the documents is to determine what that range is, how much they vary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. What sorts of things are you looking for when you compare these ranges of variations?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: You're looking for how similar or how different characters are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is this a process that's also reflected in the tick sheet or is there some other way that you would normally capture this in the process of analysing documents?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Normally you would mark on the tick sheet how similar or how different you find, but also there would be a mental approach to it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what would that mental approach be?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It would be using your experience to assess the significance of the similarities and differences that you found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So after you've conducted this comparison of the range of variations in one set of documents and the range of variations in the other set of documents, what do you do next in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: As I say, you decide how similar and how different they are and more importantly what the significance of those features are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just so that we can understand, could you give us some examples of some types of variations, whether a similarity or a difference, that would be as you say significant at this stage of the analysis.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: What I would say is, for example, there are some characters that could be similar and not necessarily be significant. For example, the letter I, which is written -- in most people just by a simple down stroke. Many people would write it in a similar way, but that wouldn't make it significant. By contrast, if in one set of writings, the Os were written in an anti-clockwise direction whereas in the other set of writing they were written in a clockwise direction, then that would be a significance between the two sets of writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, after you've compared the two sets of documents and you've undertaken this assessment process that you've explained to us, how would a forensic document examiner express their conclusions afterwards?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: There are no mathematical statistics that have yet been produced for the variations in characters, and therefore, it's not possible to express a conclusion in a numerical fashion. Therefore, document examiners use a verbal range of opinions to express their findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you as a forensic document examiner also use a range of opinions?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you explain your range of opinions.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. At the top of the scale, there would be a conclusive opinion. And by that, I mean that I think that there are sufficient similarities between two sets of writings, that they have been produced by one person and that I can exclude the possibility of another person being involved. And similarly on the negative side, there would be an opinion that two sets of writings were definitely produced by different people. In the middle, there is an inconclusive level, whereby you can't express an opinion one way or the other. However, there are also between those two extremes qualified opinions. One down from the top would be strong evidence. In this case, there would be a lot of similarities that some features that couldn't be matched, which would mean that while a conclusive opinion couldn't be given, I would consider it unlikely that anybody else has produced the writing. There is also a level of opinion which is weak evidence, whereby there are a lot of similarities but you couldn't exclude the possibility that other people who wrote in a similar fashion had produced the writing. And obviously the weak and the strong are mirrored on the negative side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. So in your analysis, just to be clear, how many levels of opinion would you give?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Seven, okay. And the seven, as you explained, represent a spectrum from -- conclusive that it is someone's handwriting and conclusive that it's not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. After you've completed your analysis and come to your conclusions, is there any sort of quality control that a forensic document examiner would undertake?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. Every case that we do is checked by a colleague to ensure that we've answered the questions that have been asked, that we haven't missed anything out, and that they agree with the findings that we've produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, if I could ask you this: Is it necessary to understand the language of a handwriting in order to conduct handwriting comparison? If you could answer simply first, if possible.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Because I've explained what we undertake is a character-by-character comparison, it's not essential to be able to understand the language to be able to compare it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you've explained to us the principles of handwriting analysis and the methodology that a forensic document examiner would go through to compare handwriting. Now, these principles and the methodology, how would they differ, if at all, in analysing handwriting in a language that the document examiner did not understand?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: The same basic principles would be undertaken, irrespective of the language that it was written in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The same basic principles. And would the same methodology also be applied?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It would indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In this case of a document -- I'm sorry, a document and a handwriting that the examiner does not understand, are there any special precautions that a document examiner should make, or are there any measures that a document examiner should apply differently?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: The main problem, if it is a language that you don't understand, is that some people write in a less legible fashion than others, and they run a lot of characters together. Now, obviously if it's a language that you can speak, generally you can work out what the characters in a word are from the context of that word. Normally only certain letters occur in certain positions, therefore you can work out what the characters are. However, if it's a language that you don't understand, you lose that ability to work out the character from its context, if you can't work out what it is from its appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You've explained to us a problem that comes up in analysing handwriting in an unknown language. Is there anything that a document examiner can do to address this issue?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Obviously you need to be able to determine the characters. And one way to do that would be to have a typed transliteration of the words you were looking at to know what characters were present in them and therefore pick them out for comparison purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, do you understand a language once referred to Serbo-Croatian and referred to here as Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yet, were you able to compare -- would you -- were you able to compare handwriting in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. It's written in Roman script, which is the same as English. So the characters are the same, and so a comparison and the basic methodologies of it, as I described, are the same within that language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is this the first time that you've examined handwriting in a language that you didn't understand?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No. I've also examined other handwritings that I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what languages were those handwritings in?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Two examples would be Dutch and Kurdish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And for whom were you doing that handwriting analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: For the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Barr, I'd like to turn now to the work that you've done for this case. You were requested by the Prosecution to conduct two comparisons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the first comparison, the questioned document were -- the questioned documents were, as we discussed earlier, the documents that are in Exhibit 133, 11 pages.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you also given another set of documents with which you were supposed to compare that first set?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I was given documents that I was told bore the specimen writing of Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And could you explain -- describe briefly those pages. How many pages of handwriting was it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I was given a personal information form, which is one page, and I was also given a book and given three entries within that book that I was told bore his specimen writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could please have the usher's assistance in placing. Just one moment, please. For the record, Your Honours, we -- the documents referred to now are Prosecutor evidence 509/B. Prosecution Exhibit 118/A and -- and Prosecution Exhibit 723 -- I'm sorry, 722.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, if you could please take a look at that -- those materials. If that's not correct, please indicate so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we seem to be having a little problem sorting these papers out. If you could just give us a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could go one document at a time, that might assist the presentation. Because the witness has been given several documents; we only have one on the ELMO. So if we could go step by step, that would probably expedite matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in fact, maybe if we could begin then taking the suggestion of Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I saw the original of this document, but I believe it was the personal information form that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And was that one of the documents you were using to compare with the questioned writing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could please ask the usher to place Prosecution Exhibit 722 on the ELMO. My mistake there. If we could next turn to Prosecution Exhibit 509/B, turning to the ERN page number 00962683.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you mean 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry it's 00760278. I was reading the English ERN number. This is the -- the proper ERN numbers there. Do you recognise that page, Dr. Barr?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That wasn't one of the ones I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. If we could place on the ELMO Prosecution Exhibit 118/A. We'll turn to the next document, please. Dr. Barr, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was that one of the pages that you were asked to examine --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: To use as a known specimen?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And next -- the next document, if we could have from that same Prosecution Exhibit, if we could turn to the next page 00760310.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, that was another one of the ones I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And for the last document, if we could just try again, on Prosecution Exhibit 509/B. And the ERN page number should be 00760278. Dr. Barr, do you also recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And was that one of the specimens that you were asked to review in comparing the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, it was, although I did see the originals rather than the photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In conducting your examination as a forensic document examiner, do you normally work with original documents?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's -- if original documents are available, it's always best to look at the original documents, because you can see far more detail than you can from a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So the material that you had before you were, as we explained earlier -- as you had described to us earlier, on the one hand you had the 11 pages, which you had described being from this workbook; and secondly, you had these four pages which you have just looked at now.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The comparison that you did between those two sets of handwriting, that led to your first report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that report was dated the 16th of July, 2003?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If the usher could please -- if I could please have the usher's assistance. It's the first report, which is marked for identification: Prosecution Exhibit 716.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, just quickly, is that your first report?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you also provide a second report --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that was date the 22nd of August, 2003?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you explain is that report to us?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I was asked to provide some more details to explain the findings my first report. I did that in my second report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance to place on the ELMO Prosecution Exhibit -- numbered for identification purposes P717.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just quickly, Dr. Barr, is that your second report?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, if we could just go through the methodology that you used in conducting this first handwriting comparison. Could you please explain to us what you did.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: As I've explained previously, the basic methodology is as I explained. I took the writing that I had been provided with as specimen writing and went through it, determining the character construction and their range of variations. I then did exactly the same thing with the questioned writing so that I had the two ranges of variations for each of the characters within the two sets of writings. I then compared them to see how similar or how different they were and then assessed the significance of those features.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is this consistent or different from the methodology you would normally follow to compare two handwritings?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And did you then come to some conclusions there?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I did, yes. What I found when I had compared the two sets of writings was that there were a lot of similarities between them; however, there were also some features within the questioned writings that I was unable to match within the specimens that I had been provided with. The presence of these differences meant that I was unable to express a definite opinion. However, the similarities were such that, in my opinion, there is strong evidence that the questioned writing was written by the writer of the specimen writing. And I considered the possibility of another person being involved is unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you explained to us earlier that you would express -- as a document examiner, you would express your opinion along a range on a scale of seven points.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Where would that opinion fall on a scale of seven points?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It would be one below the top range of opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also explained to us earlier of a problem that could come up in comparing handwriting of unknown -- of a language -- of an unknown language. Could you -- and you also explained to us some ways of addressing that problem. Could you please explain to us what, if anything, you did in this case to address that problem.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. I found in this case that the specimen writing is quite fluently written and in part is very highly connected. So determining where one character ends and another one starts does become quite difficult. However, for the purposes of my comparisons, I had been provided with books. And these books contained other entries written by other people, most of whom wrote in a far more legible style than Mr. Jokic. And also, because I'm assuming the nature of the entries, a lot of the words and phrases that appeared in his entries also appeared in other peoples' entries. And therefore, it was possible to use the other entries in the book as a means of determining -- where I couldn't decide what one of his characters was, if I found the same word in somebody else's writing that was more legible, I was then able to go back and determine what his characters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you also provided with the translation of some of that material?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I was. And again, that was a help with some of -- in particular, the block capital writing and the use of acronyms. It was possible to work out what the characters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And were you able to, on the basis that you have just explained, were you able to make out the individual character in all cases?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Not the -- there are probably some in there that I still wasn't certain of, but I did work out -- so although I wouldn't be able to work out every single one, I was able to work out a range of variation for each character.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: After you concluded your analysis, this first comparison to handwriting -- two sets of handwriting, did you continue to follow your methodology that you described earlier as regards quality control?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Would you please explain to us what was done in that regard.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: In this case my work - the statement I produced - was checked by one of my colleagues. In fact in this case it was actually, I think, checked by two of my colleagues, to be sure that they agreed with the findings that I came up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And are those two colleagues persons experienced in handwriting comparisons?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: They are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a little more detail, a little more elaboration of your findings on this first handwriting comparison. You set out some of that -- some of the basis for your conclusions in your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Would you, taking a look at the first report and the second report, just guide us to where some of that is. If we could take the first report first, and when you identify the page, please pass it to the usher so that she may place it on the ELMO. I'm sorry, is it there.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. In my first report in paragraph 5.3, I listed the page numbers and said which of the writing in there that I had found similarities between Mr. Jokic's writing and the questioned entries. And then in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Barr, if I could just stop you there. Here it appears that you go through a page-by-page assessment of the questioned pages of handwriting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry to interrupt. If you could please continue.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 5.4, which is the bottom of that page and the next page, I then explain that I found the similarities but also the features that cannot be matched, which leads me to my conclusion that there is strong but not conclusive evidence that the same person wrote the specimen and questioned writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please turn to your second report now. And when you identify the section where your findings are set out, if you could please pass that page to the usher to place on the ELMO. And, for the record, we are now looking at ERN page 03356722. Dr. Barr, if you could just tell us in brief what it is that we have there.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: As I explained, for my second report I was asked to add some more details for the reasons for my findings from my first report. In paragraph 3, I identified a number of the characters in which I found similarities between the two sets of writings, so that other people can also determine what the characters I found similar were. I've also listed in paragraph 4 the characters that were less well-matched, in particular the use of extra strokes on a number of characters that couldn't be matched. And then, in paragraph 5, which also goes on to the next page, I've indicated that my assessment -- what my assessment of those similarities and differences were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, these similarities and differences which you have set out in this second report, does that constitute the totality of your analysis, the totality of your analysis of the similarities and differences?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No. It's an indication more than that. It gives an indication of the characters I found similar or different, but obviously it's easy to write down a character and explain why it's similar or different. It's difficult to explain why I consider them significant, because that's based on my years of experience. And so -- and this one covers both the similarities and differences and my assessment of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, are you prepared today to show us in greater detail some of these similarities and differences, which you have set out here in your reports?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible for me to point out some of the similarities that I found; however, it should be borne in mind that -- because for illustration purposes, it's only really possible to compare one thing against another thing. And while that does enable everybody to see how similar or how different they are, it's not an accurate reflection of the work done, because obviously that encompasses every character and the ranges of variation. And also my experience to assess the significance of those. But it is possible to illustrate some of the features that I found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. If I understand you correctly, this will merely illustrate some of the steps that you took in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could please ask the usher's assistance in placing Prosecutor's Exhibit marked for identification P724/A. If we could please have that on the ELMO. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, what -- what is it that we have on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: On these sheets what we've got are words or phrases that have been taken from specimen and questioned writings. In each case, the one on top is in the questioned writing, and the lower one is taken from the specimen writing. They've also been enlarged to make them easier to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to point out some of these similarities and differences, which you've noted in your report and in the course of conducting your analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could please have Dr. Barr provided with a red pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, in both the questioned handwriting and this specimen that you use as a known specimen, if you could please circle the feature that you're speaking of, and then I'll ask you to write a number next to it. If you could now on the ELMO point to the first feature you'd like to show us.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: If we start with the beginning of the word, because again it illustrates quite nicely in this case the fact that a lot of the characters do run together, but at the beginning of both words we get the characters - I'll circle them - M and U. Do you want them labelled?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you just draw a small 1 next to that.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: And the same on the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. If you could circle the same and draw a small number 1 next to that as well. And what can you tell us about that comparison?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Within that, the types of things that we look for when we do a comparison with this M, you can see that you've got what we would say would be a small tick at the start of the stroke and then a large leading stroke coming up to form the start of the character. And then the M and the U are joined together in a series of very fluently written peaks to form the peaks and troughs of the M and the U.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in your assessment, is that a significant similarity for the purposes of handwriting comparison?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: As I said, yes, it's not that common a construct of an M. And as I said, it's not just the construction. What we're looking at is the fluency, the proportions, the connectiveness between them, how similar these two characters are. And in this case, we can see that it's an illustration on just these two words. You get a lot of similarities between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, could you point to another -- would you be able to point to another point of comparison on this particular page.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: On this particular page, again the ending of the word, which I will circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you could please put a 2 next to both of those circles.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Both A and A. It's more obvious on the top one. The A is a loop that actually joins over on the left-hand side, and the down stroke for it is a separate stroke. It then goes into the N, which is formed by two loops and ends with an A, which is again written as two separate -- a circle and a down stroke. And again, this can be mirrored in the bottom one, the A -- two-stroke A going into two loops and then ending with another two-stroke A. This word, as I say, does have a lot of similarities, but clearly within it if you took -- if you circled it and labelled it 3, you can see that the letter S is actually different and, as I said, we're not actually comparing that one S with that other S, I'm looking at the range of variations of the S's within both sets of writings. So there will be other examples that match between the two, however, even though they don't match in this particular word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, if I can ask you to clarify that. The -- as you say, there are differences between the S on the top which you've circled and put the number 3 next to it and the S on the bottom, also circled with a number 3. But if I understand you correctly, you're saying that's not a significant difference.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that when I looked at the S's throughout the whole bodies of writing, the variation would be matched between the two even though it's not matched in those particular words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So that in a set of questioned writing you may find a range of different S's?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That range of different S's would that include the S on the bottom -- on this page?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: The other way around because it's the specimen on the bottom. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Should we move to the next one, if I could have Prosecution Exhibit marked for identification 724/B placed on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, could you please explain what we have here.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Again, we're taking an extract from the questioned writing on the top and the specimen writing on the bottom. And to point out, for example, in the words "fornik," the construction of the letter Z.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you please circle that. Yes, thank you. Circling the Z and placing a number 4 next to it on the top and on the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Again with the letter Z, we can see clearly that it's very looped at both ends, which corresponds between the specimen and the questioned writing. And again, within this word --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Barr, if I could just ask you: Do you consider that a significant similarity for your assessment?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It is another good similarity between the two, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is there another feature you'd like to point out to us.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Another feature I found was significant between the two was within this word, the middle of the word, all the characters are in lower case, except the R which is in an upper case form. And again, you get the match between the two. Again, it's a nice matching feature between the two that wouldn't be seen in a lot of people's writings. Again, similarly --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I'm sorry. That means -- would that mean that you find that a significant similarity?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I would say each one of these significant ones isn't significant in itself, it's the totality of them that makes them significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You've explained that before. Could you expand on that a little bit, when you say that it's not significant in itself.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: As I explained when we were going through the methodology, some things are -- you will always get some things matching and some things differing between the two. And it's how you assess those similarities and its difference -- and differences that's important. And so it isn't just one character matching that leads you to come to that conclusion, it's the fact that you get many matches between the writings that enables you to come to your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So in fact it's not these specific similarities and differences. If I understand you correctly, that leads your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No, it's the totality of the similarities and differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And these are simply then illustrations of those kinds of factors that go into the totality of that comparison?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is there another feature that you'd like to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Again, within these words --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You're drawing two circles with the number 6 next to them now?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, which is the character N, which can clearly be seen to be different. However -- and don't match. However, that use of two strokes to form an N we have seen on the previous example was present in the specimen writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can we just briefly have that previous example on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: DR. BARR
utterances.text: Put that one back again within the specimen writing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down and make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters again. I'll be speaking very slowly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, you were saying that this difference -- you were explaining the difference of these two Ns.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. What I was trying to explain was that in the questioned writing on -- in the first example, the two Ns are different; however, if you look from this example of the specimen writing, you can see that the N -- it doesn't show it brilliantly because of the size of it, but again it is two loop strokes forming an N construction. And so that we can see that within the specimen writing that is a construction that does occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So -- I'm sorry, if I could just clarify -- if I could just ask you a clarification on this. Within the specimen writing, which is the writing on the bottom, you have - as you've shown us - two different types of N constructions. And you conclude from that that the difference we have on this sheet, 724/B, Prosecution 724/B, on the N which is circled and 6, that that is not a significant difference?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Would you like to go to the next sheet --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: If we just finish with this one because it also illustrates some of the features that I was unable to match. And examples of those are the use of a circle for the I dot, and these extra strokes associated with the K. Again, these are some of the features that I was unable to match that were present in the questioned writing that I was unable to match in the specimen writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Should we move on to the next sheet then. For the record, this is a sheet marked for identification P724/C.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Within this one I think if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And for the record, Dr. Barr is circling a letter on the top handwriting sample and on the bottom putting the number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: This is to show the similarities between the two letter Gs. Again, you've got -- it's constructed in two strokes, so you've got the circle forming the bowl of the G, in both cases, even in this example the fact that it starts here, comes around, and finishes sort of within the bowl of the G, as you can see is matched in the questioned. And then the tail of the G is a separate stroke, and it forms this very sort of triangular base to it. Again, it's good matches, and a lot of people -- most people do their Gs in one stroke and often have a very rounded base to them. So it's a good match between the two sets of writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you say it's a good match, does that mean that it's a significant similarity in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Maybe just a couple more examples. I'm not sure if you would want to go on the next page --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Probably quicker on the next page if we just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Barr, this next page is marked for identification P724/D. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: To speed up, if we just circle on the bottom and label it 8 in comparison with the word on the bottom and the questioned writing on the top, you can see the similarities in the narrow S joining up from the bottom to the top of the T the way the crossbar of the T joins into the A and forms a very open circle that goes straight into the G, which comes gown as a very straight line. So again, a lot of similarities between those two words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in the similarities between those two words, in your opinion, is that a significant similarity?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Well, again as we're saying -- we're building up similarities as we're going through, each one of which becomes significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps if we could stop there, unless you would like to --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: As you're saying, Dr. Barr, these are illustrations of similarities and differences, which you identified in your analysis. The Prosecution also asked you to conduct a second handwriting comparison. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The questioned handwriting there, that was the same?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What did you have as the known specimen?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I was provided with the same specimens that I've had for my first report, but I was given further specimen writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could please have the assistance of the usher in placing these pages marked for identification, Prosecution 723/A through -- /A through /K.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, do you recognise these documents?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: These are photocopies of the original writing that I was provided with as additional specimen writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're coming close to the break. Before I go into this second comparison. Would you like to take the break or should I -- it may be more convenient if we do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, how long are you going to take for your direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I would say less than 10 more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's continue and finish this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could ask you briefly, Dr. Barr, what methodology did you apply in comparing -- in conducting this comparison?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It was identical to how I've described it previously. I simply had more examples of specimen writing with which to compare the questioned writing to. And, as I've explained, because people's writing does vary from an occasion to an occasion, the more specimen writing you can get -- is generally better.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the course of carrying out your handwriting comparison in this case, did you also apply the same quality-control measures that you had in the other -- in the first handwriting comparison and in your work generally?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. There was no difference between the previous comparison or indeed any of the other comparisons that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could now have the assistance of the usher in placing on the ELMO a document marked for identification P718/A.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, what is that document?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's a copy of my third report, which was dated the 27th of January, this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And is this report based on the second handwriting comparison that you conducted?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was based on the comparison, taking into account the additional specimen writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you could please guide us to the parts of the report in which you set out your findings and your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: What I found in paragraph 2.5, the specimen writing that I'd been provided with previously contained very few block capital letters. There are more in the second bit of specimen writing. So I was able to better match the block capitals from the questioned writing to the specimen writing, which helped me to confirm my previous findings. However, the features that I marked up before, such as the circular I dot and the addition of extra strokes are still not matched within this additional specimen writing. And so I did not feel that I was able to alter my original conclusion that the number and the nature of the similarities lead me to conclude that there was strong evidence that Mr. Jokic wrote the questioned entries. However, the presence of those differences means that I can't be more certain than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So your conclusion on the seven-point scale, which you had explained to us previously, your conclusion on this report, where does that fall?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Again, it's the second down from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you've come then to the same conclusion that you came to following your first handwriting comparison?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one minute, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, on this second handwriting comparison you were provided, as you explained to us, this additional material, the, I believe, it's 11 pages of handwriting specimens. What were you told about that handwriting specimen?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I was told that it was taken from Mr. Jokic as a dictation from the 11 pages of the questioned writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Barr, are there any features about receiving these additional pages that changed your work or that had an impact on your methodology and your comparison?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Not really. It's more -- it's merely further specimen writing with which to compare the questioned with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How were -- how did you incorporate these materials into your comparison? Did you conduct the entire comparison again?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Obviously I still had my notes from the previous examination of the questioned writing, and I was also provided with the questioned writing again. In this case what I did was go through the additional specimen writing to confirm that it was consistent with the specimen writing that I'd received previously. I actually went through and drew out each character again for this additional one and made notes where I could better match things, where the matches were the same between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, you explained that your understanding is that these additional materials were handwriting -- was a handwriting specimen given when the questioned material was dictated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: To a layman, the question might come up then: Why isn't it -- why is it not identical to the questioned specimen and why are you not able to move to the highest level of conclusion that it's definitely written by Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: I'm not able to move to that highest level of opinion because, as I've explained, that there are still features within the questioned writing that aren't matched within this additional -- within the totality of the specimen writing that I've seen. However, as I've explained before, two sets of writing are never similar from one to the other, and so it doesn't surprise me that there will still be differences within the additional specimen writing, because for example writing produced on request, such as this was, generally doesn't contain the full range of variation contained within a person's handwriting, which is why we take it in addition to the previous specimen writing. And also, I am aware that there is a time difference, again which can alter why you can't match everything. And also obviously the circumstances under which this additional writing occurred is different to the circumstances within the specimen writing. And so while, as I think I said previously, the more specimen writing you've got, the better. It doesn't necessarily mean that the more you get you will always be able to match everything. There are some occasions when that's simply not going to happen for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, Dr. Barr, one person writing the same text on two different occasions, for the reasons you've explained, it wouldn't necessarily be identical?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It would never be identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It would never be identical. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we will take a break and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we have the witness, we have a ruling to make. Yesterday or the day before yesterday Mr. Karnavas informed the Bench that there's no need for him to cross-examine a witness called Ibrahimafendic. So we looked into her testimony or statement and we believe that we are in the position to admit her statement into the evidence through 92 bis. It is so decided. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, are you ready for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Regrettably I have nothing to cross on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, I'm surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not that I don't want to, but I don't think it's necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have some cross. May we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Barr, or I would rather say Dr. Barr. We don't have those resources as the OTP and we don't have an expert on handwriting, as Mr. Shin and I will have to conduct this cross-examination. First of all, I would like just to clarify one thing, because in the CV we received from the OTP it is mentioned that you finished Natural Sciences, Girton College, Cambridge University and you acquired MA or is it Bachelor of Arts, as you said?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's an MA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: MA?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before my real cross, I would like to put in front of you our case, and our case that we are not claiming that Mr. Jokic did not write portions of this operational duty officer logbook; we're just claiming that some of the portions of these entries were tampered or added later. And with your analysis and expertise, actually, you confirmed the claims of Mr. Jokic. And I will just ask you today to give us some more additional clarifications. Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just ask you about probability scale or range of options, as you named it and as it's identified within your report. Is it correct that in the field of forensic handwriting comparative analysis, examiners utilise different probability scales, as opposed to one probability scale, as identified in your expertise?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Different forensic scientists will use different scales.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you conducted one examination of Dutch handwriting. At that time, did you utilise NFI, actually Dutch system, or you utilised your own scale?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: My own scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your own scale. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Dr. Barr could be given her expertise from the 27th of January, 2004, marked as 718, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this expertise you told us today that there is seven specific levels that can be utilised by an examiner, such as yourself, in conducting these comparative analysis. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With respect to the category strong but not conclusive that you reference, it states that you consider it unlikely that another person was responsible. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still, even after reviewing the specimen, writing by Mr. Jokic - that's how we pronounce this name - you do not claim that there is conclusive evidence that Mr. Jokic is a writer?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your analysis and expertise, you found that there are some parts in the middle of this questioned writings that were not written by Mr. Jokic. And these parts you described on page 3 on your expertise from the 16th of July, 2003. And if I'm not wrong it's marked as 716. And these pages are marked by the Prosecution with numbers. So page 3 of your expertise. And there are portions marked by the OTP exhibit numbers. And if I can direct your attention to number -- fifth from the top, it's 02935747 and the next page, 02935748. Is it right that the latter portion of the first page and the top portion of the second page is not written by Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same expertise from the 16th of July, 2003, on page 3 under OTP numbers 02935745 and 02934747 you found that Mr. Jokic did not write some numbers, a part of this writing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you be so kind and take now the exhibit number P133, which is actually 11 pages of the questioned text. You have them with you?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to direct your attention to page marked as -- it's actually the fourth page marked as 02935746. Do you see that page?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Working this analysis you had a translation in front of you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a typed translation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you understand that numbers on the left-hand side actually marked time, numbers on the left-hand side --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. So I would ask you something about this number 15. On the next page marked as 02935747, as we have already established, the bottom part, the last four lines, were not written by Mr. Jokic. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first line of these four lines has number 13 or 14 in it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It seems to have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this number also represents time. Do you understand it that way?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the next page, if you can turn, marked as 02935748, after four lines that are not written, for lines on top, that are not written by Mr. Jokic, in the third line written by Mr. Jokic there is also number 15.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would ask -- I would like to ask you now if you have any explanation about this illogical time sequence represented in this document, meaning that in between 10.24 and 13 we have time marked as 15, 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's outside my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I wanted to ask you: Is it possible to establish that these two zeros in 1500 hours are not written by Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it's possible that those two numbers are not written by Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So did these differences, as added numbers, some different characteristics of letter A and H, actually protected you from expressing a definite opinion, although you had a specimen written by Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I could see from your last project written on 27th of January, this year, you had a task to compare the additional specimen handwriting in item 6 together with the handwriting detailed in paragraph 5.2 - sorry - of your report dated 16th July, 2003, with a question on pages 20935743 to 20935753 of the unofficial duty officer's logbook in order to determine whether or not there is any evidence that Dragan Jokic wrote the questioned entries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My lead counsel from this case, Mr. Stojanovic, who is not with us today, told me that it was agreed between him and Mr. McCloskey from the Prosecutor's office that you will be asked to compare the whole day of the 13th of July, 1995, which is outside of these pages. Have you been asked to do that or not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I had informed Mr. Stojanovic that anything that was any new comparisons, which is what my understanding that he was asking us about, needed to be done by his own expert, because as this expert has told us previously they don't do separate tests for different parties. And so this just came in in the last couple of days, and I did tell him that they could not do any new comparisons, that this had come up with Ms. Stojanovic -- Ms. Sinatra, because she had also, I believe, asked this company to do something, and they told her a long time ago that we can't work for both parties at the same time. It's just not how they do it. So that is what this subject has to do with. And I'm sorry Mr. Stojanovic isn't here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, maybe there's some miscommunications between your teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
